issues.legal_issue: The urgency power to take possession and dispense with an objection hearing may be used only when genuine urgency requires immediate action, not to compensate for administrative delay or inaction.
material_facts: The properties had been occupied by the government under a requisitioning law for a long time, and that law was due to cease to apply.
The authorities knew well in advance that the properties would have to be released or acquired, and had time to commence ordinary acquisition proceedings.
The government was already in possession, so there was no immediate need to take possession from the owners.
The authorities did not establish relevant material showing that completing the ordinary process, including an opportunity to object and an inquiry, would defeat the public purpose.
The delay in addressing the properties resulted from the authorities’ own laxity and failure to act in time.
issues.conclusion: The urgency power was invoked without justification, and the authorities could not dispense with the ordinary opportunity to object and inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 confer extraordinary powers that may be used only where real urgency makes it necessary to take immediate possession and dispense with the Section 5A inquiry. The authority must assess the public purpose, the actual urgency, and whether the ordinary inquiry can be completed without defeating that purpose. A public purpose alone is insufficient, and urgency cannot be used to cover administrative laxity or delay. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Gurdayal Singh, which cautioned against dispensing with an inquiry absent real urgency; Om Prakash v. State of U.P., on the significance of the Section 5A inquiry; Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra, on the need to consider whether the inquiry itself must be dispensed with; and H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra, concerning the limits of prolonged requisition.

rule.if: acquisition_case and long_term_government_occupation and advance_knowledge_of_need_to_release_or_acquire and administrative_delay and no_immediate_possession_need and no_urgent_supporting_material

predicates.acquisition_case: The government initiated compulsory acquisition of privately owned land for a public purpose.
predicates.long_term_government_occupation: The government had occupied the property for a long time before beginning the acquisition process.
predicates.advance_knowledge_of_need_to_release_or_: The acquiring authority knew in advance that it would need to release the property or acquire it permanently.
predicates.administrative_delay: The failure to take timely steps arose from delay or inaction by the acquiring authority.
predicates.no_immediate_possession_need: The government already occupied the property and did not need to take possession from the owner immediately.
predicates.no_urgent_supporting_material: The acquiring authority had no relevant material showing that following the ordinary process would defeat the public purpose.

issues.definition: When the government has occupied property for a long time, knew it would need to release or acquire it, delayed through its own inaction, does not need immediate possession, and lacks material showing that the ordinary process would defeat the purpose, it cannot dispense with the objection process.

issues.legal_issue: A notification invoking urgency is not invalid merely because it does not expressly state the nature or existence of the urgency.
material_facts: The notification referred to the urgency provision but did not state the specific urgency said to justify its use.

The Court found the notification invalid because the circumstances and available material did not establish genuine urgency, not merely because the notification omitted an express statement of urgency.
issues.conclusion: The absence of an express statement of urgency in the notification does not, by itself, invalidate it; the relevant circumstances and available records may establish whether urgency existed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(1), 17(1), and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 do not require the notification itself to recite the nature of the urgency. The existence of a proper basis for invoking the urgency power may be assessed from the surrounding circumstances and the records available when the authority formed its satisfaction. The Court relied on Union of India v. Ghanshyam Das Kedia, and distinguished the question of what the notification must recite from whether the urgency power was substantively justified.

predicates.acquisition_case: The government issued a notification as part of compulsory acquisition proceedings.
predicates.notification_omits_specific_urgency_stat: The notification does not expressly describe the urgency said to justify dispensing with the ordinary objection process.

issues.definition: In an acquisition proceeding, a notification’s omission of a specific urgency statement does not by itself invalidate the notification.

issues.legal_issue: A prior decision concerning a composite acquisition notification is binding as a precedent on the validity of its common urgency basis when the same basis applies to other properties covered by that notification.
material_facts: The properties in these appeals were covered by the same composite notification as properties considered in earlier cases.
The notification expressed a common basis for urgency in relation to all the properties, and no distinct urgency basis for the properties in these appeals was shown.
The Court had previously held that the common expression of urgency was insufficient, and that decision had not been disturbed on review.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decisions were binding precedents on the validity of the common urgency basis and applied to the properties in these appeals.
issues.legal_principle: A judgment is read in light of its facts and ratio, rather than as if it were a statute. Where a composite notification applies one common urgency basis to multiple properties, a prior ruling that the common basis is insufficient is not confined to the particular property involved in that case. The Court relied on Union of India v. Shakuntala Gupta, including its review decision, and the treatment there of Banwari Lal & Sons v. Union of India; it also distinguished the binding effect of precedent from res judicata.

rule.if: acquisition_case and composite_notification and common_urgency_basis and prior_binding_decision_rejects_common_basis and no_distinct_urgency_basis

predicates.acquisition_case: The government sought to acquire land under a notification.
predicates.common_urgency_basis: The acquiring authority relied on the same stated basis of urgency for the properties covered by the notification.
predicates.prior_binding_decision_rejects_common_ba: A prior decision of the Supreme Court rejected that common urgency basis.
predicates.no_distinct_urgency_basis: The acquiring authority did not establish a separate urgency basis for the property in the later case.

issues.definition: Where one notification covers multiple properties on a common urgency basis, a prior Supreme Court decision rejecting that basis controls if no distinct basis is established.

issues.legal_issue: A composite acquisition notification cannot be preserved for its preliminary acquisition purpose while being invalidated only insofar as it invokes the urgency power, where the common urgency foundation is invalid and that result would treat similarly situated owners differently.
material_facts: The notification covered multiple properties and relied on one common urgency basis.
The urgency basis was invalid, and the same notification had already been quashed for other owners covered by it.

Preserving the notification for the preliminary acquisition purpose while setting aside only the urgency provisions would leave the affected owners without the consequences of quashing the notification in full.
issues.conclusion: The notification could not be sustained in part by severing the urgency provisions; it was invalid as a whole.
issues.legal_principle: The common notification could not be divided so that its urgency basis was invalid for some properties but valid for others where the basis was the same. Partial invalidation would create an anomalous and unjust result, including leaving owners subject to the acquisition while removing the protections associated with the urgency process. The Court relied on the reasoning in Union of India v. Shakuntala Gupta and the earlier treatment of the same notification in Banwari Lal & Sons v. Union of India.

rule.if: acquisition_case and composite_notification and common_urgency_basis_invalid and notification_already_quashed_for_other_covered_owners

predicates.acquisition_case: The government sought to acquire land under a notification.
predicates.common_urgency_basis_invalid: The common basis relied on to invoke urgency was invalid.
predicates.notification_already_quashed_for_other_c: The same notification had already been quashed for other owners whose properties it covered.

issues.definition: When a composite notification has an invalid common urgency basis and has already been quashed for other covered owners, it cannot be preserved only in part.

issues.legal_issue: An order appointing an arbitrator to determine damages may be upheld where the same appointment was upheld in earlier cases concerning the same acquisition notification and no sufficient reason supports a different result.
material_facts: The High Court appointed an arbitrator to determine damages arising from the government’s occupation of the properties.
The appointment of an arbitrator had been upheld in earlier cases concerning the same notification.
The Court found no good reason to take a different view in these appeals and agreed that the owners should not have to begin separate civil proceedings after years of litigation.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the appointment of the arbitrator was rejected, and the appointment was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed its prior decisions upholding the arbitrator’s appointment in cases involving the same notification and found no sufficient ground for a different result. It also agreed with resolving the damages issue without requiring the owners to commence separate civil proceedings after prolonged litigation.

rule.if: acquisition_appeal and arbitrator_appointed_to_assess_occupation_damages and prior_decisions_upheld_same_appointment and no_sufficient_reason_for_different_result

predicates.acquisition_appeal: A party appealed an order made in proceedings challenging a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.arbitrator_appointed_to_assess_occupatio: The lower court appointed an arbitrator to determine damages arising from the government’s occupation of the property.
predicates.prior_decisions_upheld_same_appointment: Earlier decisions concerning the same acquisition notification upheld an arbitrator’s appointment for determining damages.
predicates.no_sufficient_reason_for_different_resul: The appealing party established no sufficient reason for treating the later appointment differently.

issues.definition: In an acquisition appeal, an arbitrator’s appointment to assess occupation damages is upheld when earlier decisions upheld the same appointment and no sufficient reason for a different result is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant with a sufficient subsisting interest in land may challenge acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: One of the challengers was a tenant of land covered by the acquisition notification.
The lower courts did not reject the tenant’s challenge as unmaintainable.
The notification was common to the properties challenged by other owners, and it was quashed in those proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s challenge could not be rejected on the categorical ground that a tenant can never challenge acquisition proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5A(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 treats as interested in land a person who would be entitled to claim an interest in compensation if the land were acquired. A tenant with a sufficient subsisting interest may therefore challenge acquisition proceedings in an appropriate case. The Court relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: A person challenges compulsory acquisition proceedings affecting land.
predicates.challenger_is_tenant: The person challenging the acquisition occupies the land as a tenant.
predicates.tenant_has_sufficient_subsisting_interes: The tenant has a continuing interest in the land sufficient to support a claim to an interest in compensation if the land is acquired.

issues.definition: A tenant may challenge an acquisition when the tenant has a sufficient subsisting interest in the affected land.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge that a writ petition should have been dismissed for delay cannot succeed in the appeal where the delay ground was not raised in that appeal and the lower courts accepted the explanation for the delay.
material_facts: The appellants argued that one writ petition should have been dismissed for delay.
The lower courts accepted the explanation for the delay and decided the petition on its merits.
The appellants did not raise the delay ground in the special leave petition in that matter.
issues.conclusion: The argument that the writ petition should have been dismissed for delay was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to accept the delay argument in light of the lower courts’ treatment of the explanation and the failure to raise the ground in the appeal. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.acquisition_appeal: A party appealed a decision in proceedings challenging compulsory acquisition.
predicates.lower_courts_accepted_delay_explanation: The lower courts accepted the explanation offered for the time taken to file the challenge.
predicates.delay_ground_not_raised_in_appeal: The appellant did not raise the delay ground in the appeal before the Supreme Court.

issues.definition: In an acquisition appeal, a delay-based challenge is rejected when the lower courts accepted the explanation for delay and the appellant did not raise that ground in the appeal.
